name: Event Loop and Call Stack
description: Understand the JavaScript event loop, call stack, and task queue.

mcqOptions.text: setTimeout(fn, 0) guarantees fn executes immediately after the current function
mcqOptions.explanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) puts fn in the macrotask queue. It executes after the current call stack clears AND any pending microtasks (Promises) complete. It's not immediate.

mcqOptions.text: Microtasks (Promise.then) execute before macrotasks (setTimeout) when both are queued
mcqOptions.explanation: After each macrotask, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before picking up the next macrotask. Promise callbacks are microtasks; setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks.

mcqOptions.text: JavaScript can execute multiple functions simultaneously on different threads
mcqOptions.explanation: JavaScript is single-threaded — it has one call stack and executes one thing at a time. Web Workers provide separate threads but don't share the main thread's scope or DOM access.

mcqOptions.text: The event loop only processes events when the call stack is empty and there are no pending microtasks
mcqOptions.explanation: The event loop processes macrotasks one at a time from the task queue when the call stack is empty. Between macrotasks, ALL pending microtasks are processed. The statement is partially right but 'no pending microtasks' is misleading.

name: Implement debounce
description: Implement a debounce function that delays invoking the provided function until after `wait` milliseconds have elapsed since the last invocation.

name: CSS Box Model
description: Understand the CSS box model and box-sizing property.

mcqOptions.text: With box-sizing: content-box, padding and border are included in the element's specified width
mcqOptions.explanation: content-box is the default — width/height only apply to the content area. Padding and border are ADDED on top, making the element larger than the specified width.

mcqOptions.text: With box-sizing: border-box, the specified width includes content, padding, and border
mcqOptions.explanation: border-box makes width/height include content + padding + border. This makes layouts more predictable — a 200px wide element is always 200px regardless of padding/border.

mcqOptions.text: Margin is included in box-sizing calculations
mcqOptions.explanation: Margin is NEVER included in box-sizing calculations for either content-box or border-box. Margin is the space outside the border.

mcqOptions.text: box-sizing: border-box is the browser default for all elements
mcqOptions.explanation: The default is content-box. Most CSS resets include `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` because border-box is more intuitive for layout.

name: Flexbox vs Grid
description: Understand when to use Flexbox vs CSS Grid for layouts.

mcqOptions.text: Flexbox is one-dimensional (row OR column) while Grid is two-dimensional (rows AND columns)
mcqOptions.explanation: Flexbox lays items out along a single axis (main axis). Grid works in both dimensions simultaneously. Use Flexbox for navigation bars, card rows; Grid for full page layouts, image galleries.

mcqOptions.text: CSS Grid cannot create responsive layouts without media queries
mcqOptions.explanation: Grid has built-in responsive features: `auto-fill`/`auto-fit` with `minmax()` creates responsive grids without media queries. E.g., `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr))`.

mcqOptions.text: Flexbox items cannot wrap to multiple lines
mcqOptions.explanation: flex-wrap: wrap allows flex items to wrap onto multiple lines. Combined with flex-basis, this creates responsive card layouts without media queries.

mcqOptions.text: You should never use Flexbox and Grid together
mcqOptions.explanation: They complement each other perfectly. A common pattern: Grid for the overall page layout, Flexbox for component-level alignment within grid cells.

name: React useEffect Cleanup
description: Understand useEffect cleanup functions and when they run.

mcqOptions.text: The cleanup function runs before the component mounts
mcqOptions.explanation: The cleanup function runs: (1) before each re-run of the effect (when dependencies change), and (2) when the component unmounts. NOT before initial mount.

mcqOptions.text: useEffect cleanup runs before the next effect execution and on unmount
mcqOptions.explanation: React runs the cleanup from the previous render's effect before running the new effect. This prevents stale closures and memory leaks from subscriptions, timers, or event listeners.

mcqOptions.text: An empty dependency array [] means the effect runs on every render
mcqOptions.explanation: [] means the effect runs ONCE after initial render (mount) and cleanup runs on unmount. No dependency array means it runs after every render.

mcqOptions.text: Cleanup functions are optional and React handles all cleanup automatically
mcqOptions.explanation: React does NOT auto-cleanup side effects. If your effect sets up a subscription, timer, or event listener, you MUST return a cleanup function to avoid memory leaks.

name: React Virtual DOM
description: Understand how React's virtual DOM and reconciliation work.

mcqOptions.text: The virtual DOM is always faster than directly manipulating the real DOM
mcqOptions.explanation: The virtual DOM adds overhead (diffing, creating virtual nodes). For simple, targeted DOM updates, direct manipulation can be faster. The virtual DOM's benefit is making complex UI updates manageable and predictable, not raw speed.

mcqOptions.text: React's reconciliation uses keys to track element identity across re-renders
mcqOptions.explanation: Keys help React identify which items changed, were added, or removed in lists. Without keys (or with index keys), React can't distinguish moved items from recreated ones, leading to incorrect state preservation or unnecessary re-renders.

mcqOptions.text: React re-renders the entire component tree when any state changes
mcqOptions.explanation: React re-renders the component where state changed and its children. But 'render' doesn't mean DOM update — React diffs virtual DOM trees and only updates changed DOM nodes. React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback can prevent unnecessary child re-renders.

mcqOptions.text: The virtual DOM is stored in the browser's memory alongside the real DOM
mcqOptions.explanation: The virtual DOM is a plain JavaScript object tree maintained by React in JS heap memory. It's not a browser API — it's React's internal representation used for diffing before committing changes to the actual browser DOM.

name: Implement throttle
description: Implement a throttle function that ensures the provided function is called at most once per `wait` milliseconds.

name: Web Vitals and Performance
description: Understand Core Web Vitals and frontend performance metrics.

mcqOptions.text: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures the time for the entire page to finish rendering
mcqOptions.explanation: LCP measures when the largest content element (image, text block) becomes visible. It's about perceived load speed, not complete render. Good LCP is under 2.5 seconds.

mcqOptions.text: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures unexpected layout movements during the page lifecycle
mcqOptions.explanation: CLS quantifies how much visible content unexpectedly shifts. Common causes: images without dimensions, dynamically injected content, web fonts causing FOIT/FOUT. Good CLS is under 0.1.

mcqOptions.text: FID (First Input Delay) measures how fast the browser renders the first pixel
mcqOptions.explanation: FID measures the delay between a user's first interaction (click, tap) and the browser's response. First pixel render is measured by FCP (First Contentful Paint). FID has been replaced by INP (Interaction to Next Paint).

mcqOptions.text: Lazy loading images always improves LCP
mcqOptions.explanation: Lazy loading above-the-fold images can HURT LCP by delaying the largest content element. Only lazy-load below-the-fold images. Use `loading='eager'` (default) for hero images.

name: Code Splitting and Lazy Loading
description: Understand code splitting strategies for frontend applications.

mcqOptions.text: React.lazy() works with server-side rendering out of the box
mcqOptions.explanation: React.lazy() only works client-side. For SSR, use a library like @loadable/component or React Server Components. React.lazy loads modules via dynamic import() which requires a browser environment.

mcqOptions.text: Route-based code splitting loads page-specific JavaScript only when the user navigates to that route
mcqOptions.explanation: By wrapping route components with React.lazy(), each page's code is in a separate chunk loaded on-demand. This dramatically reduces initial bundle size — users only download code for pages they visit.

mcqOptions.text: More code splitting always results in better performance
mcqOptions.explanation: Over-splitting creates many tiny chunks, increasing HTTP requests and adding latency from chunk loading. Each split point adds a loading state. Split at meaningful boundaries (routes, heavy libraries), not every component.

mcqOptions.text: Dynamic import() is synchronous and blocks the main thread
mcqOptions.explanation: import() is asynchronous — it returns a Promise. The module loads in the background without blocking. This is what enables lazy loading and code splitting.

name: ARIA and Semantic HTML
description: Understand web accessibility principles and ARIA attributes.

mcqOptions.text: Using ARIA attributes is always better than using semantic HTML elements
mcqOptions.explanation: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if you can use a native HTML element. <button> is better than <div role='button'> — it includes keyboard handling, focus management, and screen reader announcements for free.

mcqOptions.text: Semantic HTML elements like <nav>, <main>, <article> provide built-in accessibility landmarks
mcqOptions.explanation: Semantic elements create landmark regions that screen readers use for navigation. <nav> = navigation, <main> = main content, <aside> = complementary. Users can jump between landmarks without reading everything.

mcqOptions.text: aria-hidden='true' removes an element from the visual display
mcqOptions.explanation: aria-hidden removes elements from the accessibility tree (screen readers ignore it) but has NO effect on visual display. Use CSS display:none to hide visually. Conversely, visually-hidden CSS class hides visually but keeps in accessibility tree.

mcqOptions.text: Color alone is sufficient to convey information to all users
mcqOptions.explanation: WCAG requires that information conveyed by color is also available through other means (text, icons, patterns). ~8% of men have color vision deficiency and cannot distinguish certain color differences.

name: Keyboard Navigation
description: Understand keyboard accessibility requirements for web applications.

mcqOptions.text: All interactive elements should be reachable and operable via keyboard alone
mcqOptions.explanation: WCAG 2.1.1 requires all functionality to be available via keyboard. This means proper tab order, Enter/Space to activate, Escape to dismiss, arrow keys for composite widgets, and visible focus indicators.

mcqOptions.text: tabindex='0' makes an element the first item in the tab order
mcqOptions.explanation: tabindex='0' puts an element in the natural tab order (based on DOM position). tabindex='1' or higher sets a specific order (but is considered an anti-pattern — use DOM order instead).

mcqOptions.text: Removing the default focus outline improves accessibility
mcqOptions.explanation: The focus outline is critical for keyboard users to know which element is focused. If you remove it for aesthetics, you MUST provide an alternative visible focus indicator. :focus-visible helps — it shows focus rings only for keyboard navigation.

mcqOptions.text: Mouse-only interactions are acceptable for non-essential features
mcqOptions.explanation: WCAG requires ALL interactive features to be keyboard-accessible, not just 'essential' ones. Hover-only menus, drag-only interfaces, and click-only controls all need keyboard alternatives.

name: Implement Promise.all
description: Implement a function that behaves like Promise.all — resolves when all promises resolve, rejects on first rejection.

name: React State Management Patterns
description: Understand different state management approaches in React applications.

mcqOptions.text: Redux is required for any React application with shared state
mcqOptions.explanation: React Context + useReducer can handle shared state for many apps. Redux adds value for complex state logic, time-travel debugging, middleware, and predictable state updates at scale. But it's not always needed.

mcqOptions.text: Lifting state up is always preferable to using Context or Redux
mcqOptions.explanation: Lifting state works for closely related components. But lifting too high causes prop drilling and unnecessary re-renders of intermediate components. Context or state management libraries solve this for deeply shared state.

mcqOptions.text: Server state (API data) and client state (UI state) have different caching and synchronization needs
mcqOptions.explanation: Server state needs cache invalidation, background refetching, optimistic updates, and error retry — libraries like React Query/TanStack Query handle this. Client state (form inputs, modals, selections) doesn't need server sync and is better served by useState/useReducer.

mcqOptions.text: useContext re-renders only the components that use the changed value
mcqOptions.explanation: ALL components consuming a context re-render when ANY value in that context changes, even if they only use an unchanged part. This is why splitting contexts by update frequency and using memoization matters.

name: Implement Deep Clone
description: Implement a deep clone function that creates a complete copy of a nested object/array structure.

name: CSS Specificity
description: Understand CSS specificity rules and how styles cascade.

mcqOptions.text: An ID selector (#header) has higher specificity than any number of class selectors
mcqOptions.explanation: Specificity is calculated as (inline, IDs, classes, elements). One ID (0,1,0,0) beats any number of classes (0,0,N,0). So #header beats .nav.main.header. Only inline styles and !important override IDs.

mcqOptions.text: !important declarations follow normal specificity rules
mcqOptions.explanation: !important overrides ALL normal specificity. When two !important declarations conflict, normal specificity rules apply between them. Overusing !important creates maintenance nightmares.

mcqOptions.text: The order of CSS rules never matters if specificities are different
mcqOptions.explanation: Order matters when specificities are EQUAL — the last rule wins. When specificities differ, the more specific rule wins regardless of order. Both specificity AND source order play roles.

mcqOptions.text: Pseudo-classes like :hover have the same specificity as element selectors
mcqOptions.explanation: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :nth-child) have the same specificity as class selectors (0,0,1,0). Pseudo-elements (::before, ::after) have the same specificity as element selectors (0,0,0,1).

name: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
description: Understand CORS, preflight requests, and cross-origin security.

mcqOptions.text: CORS restrictions are enforced by the server
mcqOptions.explanation: CORS is enforced by the BROWSER. The server sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, but it's the browser that checks them and blocks the response from reaching JavaScript. Server-to-server requests are unaffected by CORS.

mcqOptions.text: A preflight OPTIONS request is sent for any cross-origin request with custom headers or non-simple methods
mcqOptions.explanation: Simple requests (GET/POST with standard headers and content types) go directly. Non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers, application/json) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request to check if the server allows the actual request.

mcqOptions.text: Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to * allows credentials (cookies) to be sent
mcqOptions.explanation: Wildcard * and credentials are mutually exclusive. To send cookies cross-origin, the server must specify the exact origin AND set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The client must also set fetch({ credentials: 'include' }).

mcqOptions.text: CORS prevents the server from receiving cross-origin requests
mcqOptions.explanation: The server ALWAYS receives and processes the request. CORS only prevents the browser from exposing the response to JavaScript. This is a common misconception — CORS is not a security mechanism for the server, it's a browser policy.
